title: Sensors Are Messengers
goals: Describe a measurement using its quantity, value, unit and conditions
Distinguish a sensor reading from an interpretation or decision
Use repeated comparisons to investigate a measurement problem without inventing certainty
vocabulary: A device that responds to a physical quantity and helps turn it into a signal
A value obtained by comparing a quantity with a scale or standard
An agreed amount used to express a quantity, such as a second or a degree Celsius
Checking and, when appropriate, adjusting a measuring system against a reference

blocks.text: Two devices are placed side by side in a shaded room and allowed to settle. At three agreed times, device A reads 20, 21 and 20 degrees C; device B reads 22, 23 and 22 degrees C. B is 2 degrees higher on every comparison. That pattern is evidence of a consistent difference under these test conditions.

We cannot conclude from agreement patterns alone that A is correct and B is wrong. A suitable checked reference can help investigate. We also need to consider whether the devices have different response times, resolutions or placement. Three comparisons in one room do not prove performance in every temperature range.

Calibration is a reference check, sometimes followed by an adjustment. Do not simply subtract 2 from every future B reading because these three pairs happened to differ by 2. A correction needs support over the conditions where it will be used.

guided_practice.title: Trace a boundary
guided_practice.prompt: A warning rule is recorded temperature greater than 28 degrees C. State its output for 27, 28 and 29 degrees C. Explain why an off warning does not prove that the sensor is working correctly.
guided_practice.answer: 27 off, 28 off, 29 on. These outputs follow the comparison applied to the recorded values. A device could report an incorrect low value while the rule correctly stays off; measurement quality needs a separate check.

independent_case.title: Investigate a new measurement dispute
independent_case.task: A classroom sound display near a speaker reads higher than one near the door. A student declares the door device broken. Propose a safe comparison using normal classroom sound. Predict one result consistent with location explaining the difference and one result that would leave a device difference worth investigating.
independent_case.answer: Place both devices side by side under the same normal sound conditions, using the same settings and reading times, or exchange positions and repeat. If readings become similar together or the higher reading follows the speaker location, location is a plausible explanation. If one device remains consistently lower side by side or after swapping, a device or setting difference remains plausible. Neither result alone proves a device broken; a checked reference and repeated observations help.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: The more stable device must be accurate
A device can repeatedly report an offset value. Stability and closeness to a reference answer different questions.
The warning proves the condition in the world
Trace the recorded number into the rule. An incorrect or irrelevant input can produce a correctly computed warning.
Missing details can be filled with sensible guesses
Keep unknown fields explicit until evidence supplies them. Guesses must be labelled as assumptions.

Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.

blocks.text: INPUT  light, sound, or heat from the environment
PROCESS  a sensor converts the signal into recorded values
OUTPUT  numbers or pixel/sound data sent to a later process
CORE IDEA  Sensors measure signals; later processing gives those signals meaning.

UNDER THE HOOD  A sensor is a transducer: it converts a physical quantity into a signal a computing system can represent. Sensing and interpretation are separate. A camera measures light; an image model may later infer a label.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
A closer explanation

blocks.title: Three different stages in a garden system
rows: Written rule checks whether value exceeds 28
Gardener decides what action is appropriate
An action or a decision to wait
blocks.caption: Sensing, checking a rule and deciding what to do are separate stages. A correct rule can still receive an unsuitable measurement.

blocks.text: The sensor responds to a physical quantity. Electronics convert the response into a recorded value. A later program can compare the value with a threshold. Nothing about this path requires us to claim that the sensor understands plant health.

The rule uses exceeds 28, so a reading of exactly 28 does not trigger it. At 29 it does. This boundary is a property of the written rule; it is separate from the question of whether the measuring device is accurate enough for the intended purpose.

blocks.title: The sensor measures. The rule decides.

Comparison picture for Microphone: air-pressure changes become samples; measurement, not understanding
Comparison picture for Thermometer: heat becomes a temperature number; measurement, not a weather decision
Comparison picture for Button: a press becomes an on/off value; a human event becomes data

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Camera  Clue: light becomes pixel values. Meaning: measurement, not meaning.
CASE 2 — Microphone  Clue: air-pressure changes become samples. Meaning: measurement, not understanding.
CASE 3 — Thermometer  Clue: heat becomes a temperature number. Meaning: measurement, not a weather decision.
CASE 4 — Button  Clue: a press becomes an on/off value. Meaning: a human event becomes data.
BOUNDARY  Do not say a sensor sees, hears, or understands. It measures and sends a representation.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
